Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> On October 5, 2023, the Biden administration's Department of Homeland Security (DHS) announced its decision to waive 26 federal laws, primarily environmental and cultural protections, to expedite the construction of a new border wall section in South Texas. Concurrently on the same day, the administration also announced the resumption of deportation flights for Venezuelan migrants back to their home country. <2> The bicameral Indigenous Peoples' Day Act was reintroduced in the U.S. Congress.; The bill proposes to designate the second Monday of October as a federal holiday.; The bill proposes to replace Columbus Day. <3> On September 8, 2023, U.S. District Chief Judge Shelly Dick ruled that Louisiana's practice of housing incarcerated children in a former death row unit at the Louisiana State Penitentiary at Angola was unconstitutional. The ruling came after a lawsuit was filed by the ACLU and other civil rights attorneys, who argued the youths were subjected to inhumane conditions, including extreme heat, extended solitary confinement, and a lack of required educational and mental health services. Judge Dick found the conditions constituted "cruel and unusual punishment" in violation of the Eighth Amendment and that the punitive atmosphere violated the Fourteenth Amendment. The state's decision to use the facility began in 2022 to house "high-risk" youths following violent incidents at other juvenile detention centers. The court ordered the state to remove all children from the Angola facility by September 15, 2023. <4> On September 5, 2023, Disability Rights Advocates (DRA) filed a lawsuit against the City of Berkeley, California, to prevent the eviction of unhoused residents from an encampment at 8th and Harrison Street. [2, 4] The lawsuit contends that the city's actions violate the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) by failing to provide sufficient and adequate alternative shelter or housing that accommodates the residents' disability-related needs. [2, 4] The legal action sought to halt the evictions until such appropriate accommodations are made available. [2, 4] Following the filing, a federal judge granted a temporary restraining order to stop the sweep of the encampment. [2] <5> The South Carolina Supreme Court, in a revised opinion, upheld a state law banning most abortions after about six weeks of pregnancy.; The ruling reversed a previous decision from earlier in the year that had blocked a similar ban. <6> In the case of Zurawski v. State of Texas, Travis County District Judge Jessica Mangrum issued a temporary injunction blocking Texas's abortion bans for individuals facing dangerous pregnancy complications. The ruling would have permitted physicians to use their "good faith judgment" to perform abortions in such medical emergencies without the risk of prosecution. However, the Texas Attorney General's office filed an immediate appeal to the state Supreme Court just hours after the injunction was issued, which automatically paused the order and prevented it from being enacted. <7> On July 26, 2023, Human Rights Watch submitted a statement for the record to the U.S. House Committee on the Judiciary, Subcommittee on Immigration Integrity, Security, and Enforcement, and the House Committee on Foreign Affairs, Subcommittee on the Western Hemisphere. The statement detailed the severe human cost of U.S. immigration deterrence policies at the U.S.-Mexico border. It argued that for three decades, policies such as the criminalization of migration, the closure of legal pathways, and attacks on the asylum system have fueled a dangerous smuggling market. Human Rights Watch specifically cited the 1994 "Prevention through Deterrence" policy, which was designed to force migrants into more hostile and dangerous terrains. The organization stated that these policies have directly led to thousands of deaths and disappearances, as well as widespread violence against migrants and asylum seekers, including injuries, kidnappings, extortion, and rape. <8> On July 26, 2023, the Michigan Supreme Court ruled in a case involving a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request for a video of a prisoner's death. The lawsuit was filed in 2017 by the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) of Michigan and Honigman LLP on behalf of freelance journalists Spencer Woodman and George Joseph, after the Michigan Department of Corrections (MDOC) denied their request for footage of a fatal altercation between prisoners. In a 5-2 decision, the court held that the journalists had fully prevailed, entitling them to recover attorneys' fees. Significantly, the court also ruled for the first time that these fees cannot be reduced on the basis that the legal work was provided pro bono. The case was remanded for a recalculation of the attorneys' fees owed by the state. <9> On July 24, 2023, the U.S. Department of Justice officially filed a lawsuit against the state of Texas and its governor, Greg Abbott, concerning the recent installation of a floating barrier in the Rio Grande river. The lawsuit demands the removal of the approximately 1,000-foot (305-meter) line of buoys, which was deployed as part of Texas's efforts to deter migrants from crossing into the U.S. from Mexico. The Justice Department alleges that Texas violated federal law by installing the barrier without obtaining the required federal authorization. The legal action explicitly cites diplomatic, humanitarian, and environmental concerns raised by the barrier's presence in the international waterway.

Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> On April 22, 2024, the U.S. Department of State's Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights, and Labor released its 2023 Country Reports on Human Rights Practices. [1, 2, 4, 5] These annual reports document human rights conditions for the calendar year 2023 in nearly 200 countries and territories. [1, 3] The reports cover internationally recognized individual, civil, political, and worker rights as defined in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and other international agreements. [2, 5] Mandated by U.S. law, the reports are submitted to Congress and are used to inform foreign policy, assistance, and the work of civil society and human rights defenders. [2, 1] In the preface, Secretary of State Antony Blinken highlighted significant human rights abuses in countries including Russia, Sudan, Iran, Afghanistan, and China, as well as the deeply troubling human rights concerns related to the conflict between Israel and Hamas. [1, 2, 6] <2> On March 19, 2024, the U.S. Supreme Court issued a ruling that allowed Texas's controversial immigration law, Senate Bill 4 (SB 4), to go into effect while legal challenges continued. [5, 10, 11] The law makes it a state crime to enter Texas from a foreign country outside of legal ports of entry and empowers state and local law enforcement to arrest and detain individuals they suspect of doing so. [8] The implementation of the law was brief, as hours after the Supreme Court's decision, the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals issued an order that once again put the law on hold. [5, 8] The Biden administration and civil rights groups, including the ACLU and the Texas Civil Rights Project, have challenged the law, arguing it unconstitutionally infringes on the federal government's authority to regulate immigration and will lead to racial profiling against Black and Brown communities. [7, 14] The case involves a complex series of legal maneuvers: a federal district court initially blocked the law, the 5th Circuit stayed that block, and the Supreme Court's decision on March 19 lifted a temporary pause on the 5th Circuit's stay, before the 5th Circuit reversed course again. [8, 9] The law, signed by Governor Greg Abbott in December 2023, remains blocked while the legal battle over its constitutionality proceeds. [3, 5] <3> On February 14, 2024, the U.S. Department of Justice announced the release of its updated Equity Action Plan, which details the department's strategies for Fiscal Year 2024 to further advance racial equity and support for underserved communities. The plan commits to five key strategies: 1. Removing barriers to grant funding for organizations serving marginalized communities; 2. Supporting corrections and reentry programs to reduce recidivism; 3. Promoting a diverse and inclusive law enforcement workforce to build public trust; 4. Improving law enforcement's response to crimes that disproportionately affect women, girls, and LGBTQ+ individuals; and 5. Enhancing language access to the department's programs and activities. <4> On February 7, 2024, Human Rights Watch released "A Human Rights Guide to the 2024 US Elections," providing key recommendations for voters, candidates, and supporters of democracy. The guide addresses a wide range of domestic and foreign policy issues, urging all candidates, regardless of party affiliation, to place human rights at the forefront of their platforms and explain how their policies will safeguard and promote them. <5> U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) announced that its total migrant encounters along the southwest border reached 302,034 in December 2023, the highest monthly total ever recorded. This figure was part of a broader nationwide total of 371,036 encounters reported by the agency for the same month. The data for the southwest border includes 249,785 encounters by the U.S. Border Patrol between ports of entry. In the first two weeks of January 2024, preliminary figures showed a decrease of over 50% in southwest border encounters between ports of entry, consistent with historical trends and enhanced enforcement measures. <6> The state of Alabama executed convicted murderer Kenneth Eugene Smith on January 25, 2024, using nitrogen gas, the first time this method of capital punishment has been used in the United States. [1] The execution took place at a South Alabama prison, and Smith was pronounced dead at 8:25 p.m. local time. [1, 4] This novel method was employed after a failed lethal injection attempt in 2022. [2, 3] Prior to the execution, the United Nations Human Rights Office warned that this untested method could amount to torture or other cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment under international human rights law. [7, 11] Following the execution, which witnesses described as involving several minutes of shaking and writhing, UN experts condemned the act, stating it was tantamount to "unethical human experimentation and was nothing short of State-sanctioned torture". [5, 6] <7> In January 2024, state legislatures saw the introduction of a significant number of anti-LGBTQ+ bills. By the middle of the month, reports indicated that over 275 to 285 such bills had been introduced. By the end of January, this number had risen to nearly 400. The proposed legislation covered a wide range of restrictions, including limiting gender-affirming medical care, censoring LGBTQ+ topics in schools, and restricting the participation of transgender youth in sports. Specifically, out of the initial wave, 71 bills pertained to healthcare restrictions, and 130 aimed to curtail students' and teachers' rights through measures like curriculum censorship and the forced outing of students. <8> Human Rights Watch released its 34th annual "World Report 2024" on January 11, 2024, providing a retrospective analysis of human rights conditions in over 100 countries during 2023. [1] The chapter on the United States highlighted that racism, anti-immigrant sentiment, and threats to democracy were significant and ongoing issues. Furthermore, the report noted a dramatic increase in the national poverty rate, which it linked to the cessation of a child tax credit implemented during the pandemic. The analysis also pointed to a rise in economic inequality and the persistence of a high racial wealth gap. <9> In a year-end report published on December 28, 2023, the NAACP celebrated a significant voting rights victory in Alabama. The pivotal moment occurred on September 26, 2023, when the U.S. Supreme Court denied Alabama's request to block a lower court's order to redraw the state's congressional map. [5] This decision upheld a federal court's rejection of a map enacted by the state legislature, which had failed to create a second congressional district with a majority or near-majority of Black voters as mandated by the Voting Rights Act. [4, 5] The Supreme Court's refusal to intervene allowed a court-appointed special master to draw a new map, which was subsequently ordered to be used in October 2023. [2] This series of events ensures that Black voters in Alabama have a fair opportunity to elect candidates of their choice in a second district, enhancing their representation in Congress. [6]

Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> On April 22, 2024, the U.S. Department of State's Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights, and Labor released its 2023 Country Reports on Human Rights Practices. [1, 2, 4, 5] These annual reports document human rights conditions for the calendar year 2023 in nearly 200 countries and territories. [1, 3] The reports cover internationally recognized individual, civil, political, and worker rights as defined in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and other international agreements. [2, 5] Mandated by U.S. law, the reports are submitted to Congress and are used to inform foreign policy, assistance, and the work of civil society and human rights defenders. [2, 1] In the preface, Secretary of State Antony Blinken highlighted significant human rights abuses in countries including Russia, Sudan, Iran, Afghanistan, and China, as well as the deeply troubling human rights concerns related to the conflict between Israel and Hamas. [1, 2, 6] <2> The Biden administration finalized new Title IX regulations on April 19, 2024, significantly expanding protections against sex-based discrimination to explicitly include sexual orientation and gender identity. [6] These new rules, which were set to take effect in August 2024, are designed to safeguard LGBTQ+ students and revise how educational institutions handle sexual assault and harassment claims. [4, 5, 6] This action reverses the policies of the Trump administration, notably those implemented by former Education Secretary Betsy DeVos, by removing the mandate for live hearings in disciplinary processes and broadening the definition of sexual harassment. [5, 6] The updated regulations clarify that sex discrimination includes discrimination based on sex stereotypes, pregnancy or related conditions, sexual orientation, and gender identity. [2] Notably, a proposed rule change regarding the participation of transgender athletes was not included in this final version and has been delayed. [6] <3> On March 19, 2024, the U.S. Supreme Court issued a ruling that allowed Texas's controversial immigration law, Senate Bill 4 (SB 4), to go into effect while legal challenges continued. [5, 10, 11] The law makes it a state crime to enter Texas from a foreign country outside of legal ports of entry and empowers state and local law enforcement to arrest and detain individuals they suspect of doing so. [8] The implementation of the law was brief, as hours after the Supreme Court's decision, the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals issued an order that once again put the law on hold. [5, 8] The Biden administration and civil rights groups, including the ACLU and the Texas Civil Rights Project, have challenged the law, arguing it unconstitutionally infringes on the federal government's authority to regulate immigration and will lead to racial profiling against Black and Brown communities. [7, 14] The case involves a complex series of legal maneuvers: a federal district court initially blocked the law, the 5th Circuit stayed that block, and the Supreme Court's decision on March 19 lifted a temporary pause on the 5th Circuit's stay, before the 5th Circuit reversed course again. [8, 9] The law, signed by Governor Greg Abbott in December 2023, remains blocked while the legal battle over its constitutionality proceeds. [3, 5] <4> On February 14, 2024, the U.S. Department of Justice announced the release of its updated Equity Action Plan, which details the department's strategies for Fiscal Year 2024 to further advance racial equity and support for underserved communities. The plan commits to five key strategies: 1. Removing barriers to grant funding for organizations serving marginalized communities; 2. Supporting corrections and reentry programs to reduce recidivism; 3. Promoting a diverse and inclusive law enforcement workforce to build public trust; 4. Improving law enforcement's response to crimes that disproportionately affect women, girls, and LGBTQ+ individuals; and 5. Enhancing language access to the department's programs and activities. <5> On February 7, 2024, Human Rights Watch released "A Human Rights Guide to the 2024 US Elections," providing key recommendations for voters, candidates, and supporters of democracy. The guide addresses a wide range of domestic and foreign policy issues, urging all candidates, regardless of party affiliation, to place human rights at the forefront of their platforms and explain how their policies will safeguard and promote them. <6> U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) announced that its total migrant encounters along the southwest border reached 302,034 in December 2023, the highest monthly total ever recorded. This figure was part of a broader nationwide total of 371,036 encounters reported by the agency for the same month. The data for the southwest border includes 249,785 encounters by the U.S. Border Patrol between ports of entry. In the first two weeks of January 2024, preliminary figures showed a decrease of over 50% in southwest border encounters between ports of entry, consistent with historical trends and enhanced enforcement measures. <7> The state of Alabama executed convicted murderer Kenneth Eugene Smith on January 25, 2024, using nitrogen gas, the first time this method of capital punishment has been used in the United States. [1] The execution took place at a South Alabama prison, and Smith was pronounced dead at 8:25 p.m. local time. [1, 4] This novel method was employed after a failed lethal injection attempt in 2022. [2, 3] Prior to the execution, the United Nations Human Rights Office warned that this untested method could amount to torture or other cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment under international human rights law. [7, 11] Following the execution, which witnesses described as involving several minutes of shaking and writhing, UN experts condemned the act, stating it was tantamount to "unethical human experimentation and was nothing short of State-sanctioned torture". [5, 6] <8> In January 2024, state legislatures saw the introduction of a significant number of anti-LGBTQ+ bills. By the middle of the month, reports indicated that over 275 to 285 such bills had been introduced. By the end of January, this number had risen to nearly 400. The proposed legislation covered a wide range of restrictions, including limiting gender-affirming medical care, censoring LGBTQ+ topics in schools, and restricting the participation of transgender youth in sports. Specifically, out of the initial wave, 71 bills pertained to healthcare restrictions, and 130 aimed to curtail students' and teachers' rights through measures like curriculum censorship and the forced outing of students. <9> Human Rights Watch released its 34th annual "World Report 2024" on January 11, 2024, providing a retrospective analysis of human rights conditions in over 100 countries during 2023. [1] The chapter on the United States highlighted that racism, anti-immigrant sentiment, and threats to democracy were significant and ongoing issues. Furthermore, the report noted a dramatic increase in the national poverty rate, which it linked to the cessation of a child tax credit implemented during the pandemic. The analysis also pointed to a rise in economic inequality and the persistence of a high racial wealth gap. <10> In a year-end report published on December 28, 2023, the NAACP celebrated a significant voting rights victory in Alabama. The pivotal moment occurred on September 26, 2023, when the U.S. Supreme Court denied Alabama's request to block a lower court's order to redraw the state's congressional map. [5] This decision upheld a federal court's rejection of a map enacted by the state legislature, which had failed to create a second congressional district with a majority or near-majority of Black voters as mandated by the Voting Rights Act. [4, 5] The Supreme Court's refusal to intervene allowed a court-appointed special master to draw a new map, which was subsequently ordered to be used in October 2023. [2] This series of events ensures that Black voters in Alabama have a fair opportunity to elect candidates of their choice in a second district, enhancing their representation in Congress. [6]
